parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Explain what is meant by the photoelectric effect.

markscheme_points.text: electromagnetic radiation/photons incident on a surface
causes emission of electrons (from the surface)

hints: Hint 1: Think about the two sides of the story - what type of energy is arriving at the metal, and what type of particle lives inside the metal that could escape.
Hint 2: To get full credit, make clear that light arrives as photons on a surface and the result is electrons leaving that surface, not just general excitation.
parts.proper_answer: Electromagnetic radiation (photons) incident on a metal surface causes the emission of electrons from the surface.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture Light as Photons Hitting Metal**
Think of light not as a continuous wave here but as a stream of tiny packets of energy called photons. These photons travel to and strike a clean metal surface.

Step 2: **Picture Electrons Being Knocked Out**
If a photon has enough energy, its whole energy is given to one electron in the metal. That electron can then escape from the surface. That release of electrons by incident light is the photoelectric effect.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
One wavelength of electromagnetic radiation emitted from a mercury vapour lamp is $436\text{ nm}$.

Calculate the photon energy corresponding to this wavelength.
hints: Hint 1: Recall how the energy carried by a single packet of light depends on its wavelength - shorter wavelength means higher frequency and higher energy, linked by two fundamental constants.
Hint 2: Check your wavelength is in metres ($436 \text{ nm} = 436 \times 10^{-9} \text{ m}$) before you combine the constants to get energy in joules.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Choose the Photon Energy Law**
You know wavelength, you want energy of one photon. The link is: $$E = \frac{hc}{\lambda}$$ where $h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \text{ J s}$ and $c = 3.00 \times 10^{8} \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

Step 2: **Convert and Substitute**
Convert $\lambda = 436 \text{ nm} = 436 \times 10^{-9} \text{ m}$. Then: $$E = \frac{(6.63 \times 10^{-34})(3.00 \times 10^{8})}{436 \times 10^{-9}}$$ $$E = 4.56 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J}$$ This is about $2.85 \text{ eV}$, a typical blue photon energy.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.part_stem:
Light from the lamp in (b) is incident, separately, on the surfaces of caesium and tungsten metal.

Data for the work function energies of caesium and tungsten metal are given in Fig. 10.1.

{{figure:figure_10_1}}

Calculate the threshold wavelength for photoelectric emission from
hints: Hint 1: Remember what threshold means - it is the longest wavelength (lowest frequency) that can still just release an electron, when photon energy exactly equals the minimum escape energy.
Hint 2: Convert the work function from eV to J using $1 \text{ eV} = 1.60 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J}$, then rearrange $\Phi = hc/\lambda_{0}$ to find $\lambda_{0}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link Work Function to Threshold**
At threshold, the photon just has enough energy to free an electron with zero kinetic energy left over. So: $$\Phi = \frac{hc}{\lambda_{0}}$$ where $\Phi$ is the work function and $\lambda_{0}$ is the threshold wavelength.

Step 2: **Convert eV to J and Calculate**
For caesium, $\Phi = 1.4 \text{ eV} = 1.4 \times 1.60 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J} = 2.24 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J}$. Rearrange for wavelength: $$\lambda_{0} = \frac{hc}{\Phi} = \frac{(6.63 \times 10^{-34})(3.00 \times 10^{8})}{1.4 \times 1.60 \times 10^{-19}}$$ $$\lambda_{0} = 8.88 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m} \approx 890 \text{ nm}$$ This is in the near infra-red.

hints: Hint 1: Use exactly the same method as for caesium, but now with the larger work function of $4.5 \text{ eV}$ for tungsten - expect a much shorter threshold wavelength.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: Use your answers in (c) to state and explain whether the radiation from the mercury lamp of wavelength $436\text{ nm}$ will give rise to photoelectric emission from each of the metals.

markscheme_points.text: caesium: wavelength of photon less than threshold wavelength (or v.v.) or $\lambda_{0} = 890 \text{nm} > 436 \text{nm}$ so yes
tungsten: wavelength of photon greater than threshold wavelength (or v.v.) or $\lambda_{0} = 280 \text{nm} < 436 \text{nm}$ so no

hints: Hint 1: Think in terms of energy - emission happens only if the incoming $436 \text{ nm}$ photon has more energy than the work function, which is the same as asking if $436 \text{ nm}$ is shorter than the threshold wavelength.

Hint 2: Compare $436 \text{ nm}$ separately with $890 \text{ nm}$ for caesium and $280 \text{ nm}$ for tungsten to decide yes or no for each, remembering shorter wavelength means higher photon energy.
parts.proper_answer: Caesium: yes, emission occurs because $436 \text{ nm} < 890 \text{ nm}$, photon energy > work function. Tungsten: no emission because $436 \text{ nm} > 280 \text{ nm}$, photon energy < work function.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use the Wavelength Rule**
Shorter wavelength means higher photon energy. For emission you need $\lambda_{photon} \le \lambda_{0}$, equivalently photon energy $\ge$ work function.

Step 2: **Apply to Both Metals**
Caesium: $\lambda_{0} = 890 \text{ nm} > 436 \text{ nm}$. The incident photon is shorter than threshold, so it has more than enough energy. Yes, electrons are emitted.
Tungsten: $\lambda_{0} = 280 \text{ nm} < 436 \text{ nm}$. The incident photon is longer than threshold, so its energy $4.56 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J}$ is less than the $4.5 \text{ eV}$ work function. No, electrons are not emitted.
